newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan orders bank to halt operations.
newsitem.headline: Japan orders bank to halt operations.

text.p: Japan's financial authorities on Thursday ordered a bank to halt most operations, the first time in the postwar era that government regulators have taken such a step.

A senior Finance Ministry official told Reuters that Hanwa Bank Ltd, a second-tier regional bank, was ordered to suspend all its operations except deposit withdrawals because it was unable to recover bad loans.

Japanese government bonds opened higher on the news, as traders said the Bank of Japan would have little option but to keep its ultra-easy credit stance to cope with the the bad loan problems at other regional banks.
Tokyo stocks opened a bit higher. Brokers said the Hanwa news was no real surprise and financial system woes had largely been factored into prices.
Hanwa, employing about 900 people, operates mostly around the city of Osaka in western Japan.

It is only Japan's third bank failure since World War Two. The two other failures, one last year and one this year, were handled by the creation of new banks to take over the failed institutions' business, but Hanwa looked set to be completely liquidated, domestic media said.
The Finance Ministry official said details of Hanwa's troubles would be announced at a news conference later on Thursday, but added that the bank's depositors would be fully protected.
Established in 1941, Hanwa has book assets of about 658 billion yen ($5.92 billion). It is not one of Japan's "big 20" first-tier national banks.

Hanwa Bank -- like much of Japan's financial system -- has been hard hit by the collapse of real estate prices from the sky-high levels of the 1980s "bubble" era, when property and share prices soared.

"The ministry made the decision following the judgment that Hanwa Bank will most likely incur about 30 billion yen ($270 million) in liabilities, or an excess of liabilities over assets, in the (April-September) first half of fiscal 1996/97, making it extremely difficult to turn around on its own," Kyodo news agency said.
Hanwa announced on November 5 that it had revised its forecast for parent current earnings for the six months to September to a loss of 280 million yen ($2.52 million).

Previously, the bank had forecast a parent current profit of 60 million yen ($540,000) for the first half of fiscal 1996/97, against an actual 232 million yen ($2.09 million) in current profit a year earlier. But in 1995/96, ended March 31, it posted a current loss of 6.55 billion yen ($59.0 million).
Current profit is pre-tax, including profits or losses from stock selling and other non-banking business.
Last year Japan suffered its first bank failure since the war when Hyogo Bank, based in Kobe, also in western Japan, fell victim to bad loans.

The news of Hanwa Bank's shutdown helped boost the dollar in New York, where the greenback had earlier dipped below 111 yen on the back of a wider U.S. trade deficit. It then recovered to 111.70 yen after news of Hanwa's shutdown as traders speculated that Japan's central bank would keep interest rates low to help the country's financial institutions.
Stock market pundits had expected share prices to come under pressure from the news but said a plunge was unlikely given that Japan's financial system woes are well-known.
"Investors have started separating the good apples from the bad," said Hiroshi Morimoto, general manager at Daiwa Securities.
"The suspension news should not discourage them too much because in a way, the government is helping them by weeding out the companies which are faltering," he added. ($1=111 yen)
